text: Design a hash map without using a built-in hash table. Implement put, which takes a key and a value; get, which returns the value, or negative one if the key is absent; and remove.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — what are the ranges of the key and the value? And does put on an existing key update it?
Both key and value are from zero to ten to the sixth, and yes, put updates.

Two things stand out. The key is bounded, so I can direct-address, the same way a hash set would — but now each slot holds a value, not a boolean. And the value is non-negative, so I can use negative one as a sentinel for no mapping. It's basically a hash set with bool swapped for int.

Let me think about the sentinel. This problem reminds me of direct addressing: when keys are small, dense integers, the key itself can be the array index, so there's no hashing and no collisions. A set marks present with a bit; a map has to store the value and still tell absent apart. Since values are at least zero, filling the array with negative one gives a clean absent marker that no real value can collide with. If get reads negative one, the key was never put. One thing worth flagging — it all rides on values being at least zero. If values could be negative one, I'd need a separate presence array.

Here's the plan. One: one int array of size ten to the sixth plus one, all set to negative one. Two: put just writes the slot, so insert and update are the same operation. Three: get returns the slot, and remove writes negative one back. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The constructor fills one million and one slots with negative one, and each method is a single array access. The size is the line that's easy to get wrong: keys go up to ten to the sixth inclusive, so the array needs one million and one slots, or the largest key goes out of bounds. Every operation is constant time, and put handles insert and update identically — it just overwrites the slot.
What if the value could be any integer, including negative one?

Then a single sentinel breaks — putting negative one would be indistinguishable from absent. I'd split existence from value with a parallel presence array. Now the value can be anything — the boolean carries existence separately. And for unbounded keys, I'd use buckets of key-value pairs, indexed by key mod a prime, where put scans the bucket to update or insert — that's an unordered map in miniature.

Let's trace update and remove. Put one, one, then get one returns one, and get three returns negative one, since it was never put. The row that matters is the last one: put two, overwrite it, then remove two — get two returns negative one. Never put and put then removed both return negative one. For a map both are absent, so the shared sentinel is correct.

Direct addressing is constant time per operation. Space is proportional to the key range — an int array of ten to the sixth is about four megabytes, thirty-two times a bit-packed hash set's hundred and twenty-five kilobytes, because each slot holds a thirty-two-bit int instead of one bit. Oh, one more thing — a set is just a map whose value is one bit. And whenever the key range is small and dense, a plain array beats a hash map — no hashing, no collisions, cache-friendly, worst-case constant time. That's exactly why anagram-style problems use an int count array of twenty-six. The array is the map when keys are indices.

Excellent. You reused the direct-address idea, picked negative one as the sentinel with the values-at-least-zero justification, and knew the presence-array fallback and the bucket generalization. Clean.
